projects.name: Analytics Dashboard Platform
projects.description:
End-to-end analytics dashboard initiative covering three data domains and a delivery layer:

1) CUSTOMER CSV PROCESSING — ingest, validate, clean, transform, and store customer data from recurring CSV drops; establish schema contracts and data-quality gates.
2) APPLICATION LOG ANALYSIS — parse, normalize, enrich, index, and query application logs to produce usage, error, and performance metrics.
3) VISUALIZATION COMPONENTS — build a reusable charting/design layer, dashboard composition (layout, filters, cross-filtering), accessibility, and rendering performance.
4) INTEGRATION, SECURITY & DELIVERY — shared API layer, authentication/role-based access, orchestration, performance/caching, CI/CD, observability, and rollout.

Structure: four milestones (parent tasks) decomposed into sprint-sized subtasks scoped to roughly 1-3 days each, with explicit acceptance criteria and dependencies so no single work item is too large or ambiguous to execute.

Tags: analytics, dashboard, data-engineering, csv-processing, log-analysis, visualization, milestones

tasks.name: M1 — Customer CSV Data Processing Pipeline
tasks.details:
MILESTONE 1 GOAL: Turn recurring customer CSV files into a validated, queryable analytics dataset.

Scope:
- Define and version the CSV schema contract (column names, types, nullability, allowed values).
- Implement file intake (drop folder / object storage trigger), checksum-based idempotency, and archive of raw originals.
- Build validation + quarantine flow with row-level error reporting.
- Implement cleaning/normalization, deduplication, and type coercion.
- Load into the analytics storage layer with a documented star/flat schema.
- Add incremental load strategy (watermark on updated_at / file manifest).
- Add data-quality monitoring, freshness SLIs, and alerting.

Exit criteria:
- A new CSV drop flows end-to-end to queryable tables without manual steps.
- Malformed rows are quarantined with a readable error report; valid rows still load.
- Row counts reconcile between source file and target table.
- Schema changes are caught before load, not after.

Dependencies: none (can start immediately). Feeds M3 and M4.

tasks.name: M2 — Application Log Analysis Pipeline
tasks.details:
MILESTONE 2 GOAL: Turn raw application logs into structured event metrics that the dashboard can chart.

Scope:
- Inventory log sources (services, files, stdout, log shipper) and document formats (JSON lines, plain text, syslog).
- Define the canonical event schema (timestamp, service, level, request_id, user/customer id, latency, status, message).
- Build parsers per format with a fixture-based test suite.
- Normalize severity levels, timezones→UTC, and enrich with service/team/environment dimensions.
- Route to storage (search index or columnar table) with retention policy.
- Build aggregation queries/views: error rate, p95/p99 latency, request volume, top error signatures.
- Add parsing-failure dead-letter queue with visibility.

Exit criteria:
- All in-scope log sources parse with >99% success on a 7-day sample.
- Unparsed lines land in a DLQ and are inspectable.
- Aggregation views return error rate and latency percentiles for any time range in <5s.
- Retention + partition strategy documented and implemented.

Dependencies: none (parallel to M1). Feeds M3 and M4.

tasks.name: M3 — Visualization Component Library & Dashboards
tasks.details:
MILESTONE 3 GOAL: Deliver a reusable, accessible visualization layer and the dashboard screens that use it.

Scope:
- Select charting foundation and document the decision (library, bundle size, SSR support).
- Define design tokens (color scales, typography, spacing) and chart theming.
- Build reusable primitives: line/time-series, bar, stacked bar, KPI/stat tile, table, sparkline, heatmap.
- Build shared states: loading skeleton, empty, error, partial-data.
- Dashboard composition: responsive grid layout, filter bar (date range, service, customer segment), cross-filtering.
- Data-fetching/state layer wired to the M1/M2 query APIs, with caching and request de-duplication.
- Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA: contrast, keyboard, screen-reader summaries) and responsive breakpoints.
- Render performance budget and snapshot/interaction tests.

Exit criteria:
- Every chart primitive is documented in a component gallery with props and examples.
- Dashboards render correctly at 375px, 768px, and 1440px widths.
- All charts pass automated accessibility checks and keyboard navigation.
- Initial dashboard load meets the agreed performance budget on a throttled connection.

Dependencies: needs at least one query API from M1 or M2 for live data, but component work can begin immediately with mocks. Feeds M4.

tasks.name: M4 — Integration, Security, Operations & Launch
tasks.details:
MILESTONE 4 GOAL: Make the dashboard a production service people can trust and operate.

Scope:
- Unified query/API gateway in front of M1 and M2 storage (consistent params, pagination, timeouts).
- Authentication and role-based access control (viewer / analyst / admin), including row-level scoping for customer data.
- Environment strategy: dev / staging / prod with seeded sample data.
- Caching and query performance tuning against realistic volumes.
- CI/CD pipeline: build, test, migrate, deploy, rollback.
- Observability for the dashboard itself: uptime, query latency, error rate, data freshness panel.
- Runbook, on-call escalation, and user-facing launch documentation.

Exit criteria:
- Staging mirrors production config and passes the end-to-end smoke suite.
- Access control verified by tests for each role and scope.
- One-click (or one-pipeline) deploy with tested rollback.
- Data-freshness and query-latency alerts fire correctly in a drill.
- Runbook reviewed with the on-call owner; launch notes published.

Dependencies: M3 for the UI, M1/M2 for the data. Can start auth/CI/CD foundations early in parallel.

tasks.name: M1.1 Define & profile CSV schema contract
tasks.details:
OBJ: Produce a written, versioned contract for customer CSV files that ingestion code and upstream producers both reference.

STEPS:
1. Collect 3-5 representative CSV samples covering different customer segments and dates.
2. Profile every column: inferred type, null %, distinct count, min/max, format anomalies (dates, currency, whitespace, encoding).
3. Write schema spec: column name, logical type, required/optional, max length, allowed enum values, PII classification.
4. Define the versioning rule: additive columns = minor bump; renamed/removed/type-changed = major bump requiring consumer update.
5. Store as a machine-readable file (e.g. schema.yaml) checked into the repo + a human-readable README.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Every column in the samples is accounted for with a documented type and nullability.
- A reviewer can read the spec and predict what a valid file looks like.
- Spec is machine-loadable by the validator built in the next task.

SIZE: ~1-1.5 days. Independent; unblocks validation work.

tasks.name: M1.2 Build file intake, archive & idempotency
tasks.details:
OBJ: A reliable, idempotent way for CSV files to arrive in the system exactly once.

STEPS:
1. Choose intake mechanism (scheduled poll of a drop folder vs object-storage event notification). Document the tradeoff.
2. Implement file discovery + copy of the raw original to an immutable archive path (partitioned by ingest date).
3. Compute SHA-256 checksum; maintain an ingest manifest table (filename, checksum, size, row_count, status, ingested_at).
4. Reject/log duplicates by checksum instead of re-loading them.
5. Emit a structured "file received" event that downstream steps consume.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Dropping the same file twice results in exactly one ingest record and no duplicate data.
- Raw originals are retrievable by date after processing.
- A corrupt/zero-byte file fails fast with a clear log line, without creating a manifest row marked success.

SIZE: ~1-2 days. Depends on M1.1 only for file naming conventions.

tasks.name: M1.3 Implement validation rules & quarantine flow
tasks.details:
OBJ: Reject bad data loudly and precisely, without blocking good rows.

STEPS:
1. Load schema.yaml from M1.1 and validate: required headers, unexpected/missing columns, type parseability, enum membership, length limits, cross-field rules (e.g. end_date >= start_date).
2. Implement two-tier policy: file-level failures (bad headers, truncated file) stop the whole load; row-level failures quarantine only that row.
3. Write invalid rows to a quarantine table with: source file, row number, failing rule(s), raw row payload.
4. Produce a per-run validation report (counts valid / quarantined / reasons histogram).
5. Add unit tests with fixture CSVs for each failure mode.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A file with 1 bad row out of 1000 loads 999 rows and quarantines 1 with the exact reason.
- A file with a missing required column is rejected with a message naming the column.
- Quarantine rows are queryable and link back to the source file.

SIZE: ~2-3 days. Depends on M1.1.

tasks.name: M1.4 Cleaning, normalization & deduplication
tasks.details:
OBJ: Convert validated raw rows into consistent, analytics-ready records.

STEPS:
1. Normalize text: trim whitespace, standardize casing for enums, collapse internal whitespace.
2. Coerce types: ISO-8601 dates in UTC, decimals for currency (no floats), integers for counts.
3. Standardize identifiers (customer_id canonical form, email lowercased).
4. Deduplicate on the business key; define deterministic "latest wins" by updated_at then row order.
5. Handle nulls per schema policy (default value vs reject vs keep null).
6. Output a cleaned intermediate table; keep raw values for audit.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Running the transform twice on the same input produces identical output (deterministic).
- Date, currency and ID fields conform to the documented types in 100% of non-quarantined rows.
- Duplicate business keys collapse to one row with the documented winner.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on M1.1 and M1.3.

tasks.name: M1.5 Design & implement analytics storage schema
tasks.details:
OBJ: Land cleaned customer data in a documented schema the dashboard can query efficiently.

STEPS:
1. Design tables: a core customer dimension, plus fact tables for the measures the dashboard needs (e.g. activity, revenue, segment).
2. Choose grain and keys for each table; document in a simple ERD + column dictionary.
3. Write DDL/migrations that are idempotent and runnable in CI.
4. Load from the M1.4 intermediate output using merge/upsert on the business key.
5. Add indexes/clustering on the columns used by dashboard filters (date, segment, customer_id).
6. Verify with reconciliation queries: source row count == target row count for a full refresh.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Schema documented with grain, keys, and column meanings.
- Migrations run cleanly from empty on a fresh database.
- Dashboard-shaped filter queries (date range + segment) return in under 2s on a realistic volume.

SIZE: ~2-3 days. Depends on M1.4.

tasks.name: M1.6 Incremental load & scheduling
tasks.details:
OBJ: Only load new/changed data, reliably, on a schedule.

STEPS:
1. Pick the watermark strategy: max(updated_at) per source, or file-manifest-driven batch ranges. Document choice.
2. Implement the watermark store (table or state file) with atomic update after a successful commit.
3. Implement upsert semantics so re-runs are safe: late-arriving rows and retroactive edits both land correctly.
4. Wire the scheduler (cron/airflow/managed job) with a single entrypoint and clear exit codes.
5. Add a "full refresh" path for recovery, guarded behind an explicit flag.
6. Test with out-of-order files and a replayed old file.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A replayed old file does not duplicate rows or revert newer values.
- Incremental run on unchanged data loads 0 rows and completes quickly.
- Failure mid-run leaves the watermark unchanged so the next run retries the same window.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on M1.2 and M1.5.

tasks.name: M1.7 Data quality monitoring & freshness alerts
tasks.details:
OBJ: Know when customer data is stale, missing, or drifting — before a dashboard user notices.

STEPS:
1. Define SLIs: freshness (age of newest loaded row), volume (rows vs 7-day trailing average), null-rate per critical column, quarantine rate.
2. Implement the checks as scheduled queries writing to a metrics table.
3. Define thresholds and alert routing (channel + severity), with a suppression window to avoid alert storms.
4. Add a compact data-quality summary view the dashboard itself can display.
5. Run one deliberate failure drill (drop a file / send a bad schema) and confirm the alert fires.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Each SLI is computed automatically on a schedule and visible historically.
- A simulated 2x missed schedule produces exactly one alert, not a flood.
- Thresholds are documented with rationale and are easy to tune.

SIZE: ~1.5-2 days. Depends on M1.3 and M1.6.

tasks.name: M2.1 Inventory log sources & formats
tasks.details:
OBJ: Know exactly what log data exists and what it looks like before writing parsers.

STEPS:
1. Enumerate every log source: services, file paths/streams, log shipper, environments.
2. For each, capture 200-500 sample lines covering normal traffic, errors, timeouts, and startup/shutdown.
3. Classify format: JSON lines, key=value, plain text with regex, syslog, multi-line stack traces.
4. Note volumes (lines/day), growth rate, and peak burst — this drives retention and partitioning later.
5. Document known gaps: missing request ids, inconsistent field names across services, PII present in messages.
6. Write a source inventory table + a parser priority order (highest volume/highest value first).

ACCEPTANCE:
- Every source has a named owner, format classification, sample set, and daily volume estimate.
- Multi-line log events (stack traces) are explicitly identified.
- PII presence is flagged per source as a compliance input.

SIZE: ~1-2 days. Independent; unblocks all parser work.

tasks.name: M2.2 Define canonical log event schema
tasks.details:
OBJ: One agreed event shape that every parser outputs and every query consumes.

STEPS:
1. Define required fields: event_time (UTC), service, environment, severity (canonical set), message, request_id, trace_id.
2. Define optional fields: customer_id, user_id, http_status, latency_ms, route, error_code, error_signature.
3. Fix the severity mapping table (e.g. WARN/WARNING→warn, FATAL/CRIT→fatal) so cross-service comparisons are valid.
4. Specify types, units, and null semantics for each field; state that timestamps are UTC ISO-8601 with ms precision.
5. Publish as a versioned schema doc + a typed struct/model in code.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A developer can implement a new parser from this doc alone.
- Severity mapping covers every value observed in M2.1 samples.
- Field names and units are unambiguous (latency explicitly milliseconds).

SIZE: ~1 day. Depends on M2.1.

tasks.name: M2.3 Implement per-format log parsers + fixtures
tasks.details:
COORDINATION TICKET (not directly executable). Scope was too large for one work item, so it is split into:

- M2.3a Parser framework + JSON-lines parser (12h)
- M2.3b Key=value, regex & multi-line parsers + fixtures (12h)

Done when both children meet their acceptance criteria and the parsers are wired into the ingest path from M2.5.

tasks.name: M2.4 Normalization, enrichment & PII redaction
tasks.details:
OBJ: Add the dimensions the dashboard needs to slice logs by, and scrub sensitive data.

STEPS:
1. Map service → team and service → tier via a small lookup config (not hardcoded).
2. Derive dimensions: environment (prod/staging/dev), region if present, normalized route (strip ids from paths), status class (2xx/4xx/5xx).
3. Compute error_signature: normalize messages by replacing ids/numbers/uuids so similar errors group together.
4. Redact PII patterns (emails, tokens, card-like numbers, session ids) before storage; keep a redaction counter.
5. Add unit tests for the redaction patterns and the route/error normalization.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Same logical error with different ids produces one identical error_signature.
- Redaction tests cover each pattern and confirm no false positives on typical log lines.
- Enrichment config is editable without a code deploy.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on M2.2 and M2.3.

tasks.name: M2.5 Log storage, partitioning & retention
tasks.details:
OBJ: Store normalized events with sensible partitioning, retention, and query speed.

STEPS:
1. Choose the store based on M2.1 volumes: search index (fast text) vs columnar table (cheap aggregation). Document the tradeoff.
2. Define partitioning: by day (and hour if volume is high); define sort/cluster keys on service + severity + event_time.
3. Implement retention: hot 30 days, warm 90 days archive to object storage, hard delete beyond policy.
4. Add a lifecycle job that enforces retention and reports bytes reclaimed.
5. Load test with a realistic 7-day backfill and record index size + ingest throughput.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A 7-day backfill completes within the agreed window and the store stays queryable during load.
- Retention job dry-run correctly identifies expired partitions.
- Storage cost estimate documented per month at projected growth.

SIZE: ~2-3 days. Depends on M2.3 and M2.4.

tasks.name: M2.6 Build aggregation metrics & query views
tasks.details:
COORDINATION TICKET (not directly executable). Split into:

- M2.6a Metric definitions & raw aggregation queries (12h)
- M2.6b Summary tables, percentile correctness & query tests (10h)

Done when every dashboard metric is defined, queryable under the 5s budget for a 30-day range, and covered by fixture tests.

tasks.name: M2.7 Parse-failure dead-letter queue & replay
tasks.details:
OBJ: No log line silently disappears — unparsable input is captured and visible.

STEPS:
1. Define the DLQ record: source, received_at, raw payload (bounded length), error code, error message, parser version.
2. Route all parse failures to the DLQ instead of dropping or crashing.
3. Add a simple inspection path (query/view) plus a daily count metric.
4. Alert when DLQ volume exceeds a percentage of total ingest (e.g. >1%).
5. Add a replay tool that re-runs DLQ records through a fixed parser version.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Deliberately corrupt an input file and confirm 100% of its lines appear in the DLQ.
- DLQ rate is chartable and alerts on threshold breach.
- Replay of a fixed parser reprocesses DLQ records and removes them from the queue on success.

SIZE: ~1.5-2 days. Depends on M2.3.

tasks.name: M3.1 Charting library evaluation & ADR
tasks.details:
OBJ: A written decision on the charting foundation, so component work starts on solid ground.

STEPS:
1. List candidate approaches (e.g. Recharts, visx, ECharts, D3, Observable Plot) plus a "build on primitives" option.
2. Score each against: bundle size, SSR/hydration support, accessibility story, canvas vs SVG, time-series performance at 10k+ points, license, maintenance activity.
3. Build a 30-line throwaway spike for the top 2 candidates rendering the same time-series chart.
4. Record the decision in a short ADR: chosen option, rejected options, and the conditions that would reverse it.

ACCEPTANCE:
- ADR merged with a clear winner and rationale.
- Bundle-size impact measured, not guessed.
- Team can explain why the alternative was rejected.

SIZE: ~1 day. Independent; gates everything else in M3.

tasks.name: M3.2 Design tokens & accessible chart theming
tasks.details:
OBJ: A shared visual language so charts look consistent and pass contrast checks.

STEPS:
1. Define tokens: neutral scale, sequential palette (for heatmaps), categorical palette (max 8 series, colorblind-safe), semantic colors (ok/warn/error).
2. Verify every text/background and series/background pairing against WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1 text, 3:1 graphical).
3. Define typography scale, spacing unit, chart margins, axis/gridline weights, tooltip and legend styles.
4. Implement tokens as CSS variables + a typed theme object shared by all charts.
5. Add a visual token reference page rendering the palette with contrast ratios displayed.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Palette passes automated contrast checks; ratios are visible in the reference page.
- Categorical colors remain distinguishable in a grayscale/simulated-deuteranopia check.
- Charts consume tokens only — no hardcoded hex values in components.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M3.1.

tasks.name: M3.3 Build core chart primitives
tasks.details:
COORDINATION TICKET (not directly executable). Seven components was too much for one work item, so it is split into:

- M3.3a TimeSeries, Bar & KPI tile primitives (12h)
- M3.3b DataTable, Sparkline & Heatmap primitives (12h)

Done when all seven primitives are in the gallery, typed, and render all shared states from M3.4.

tasks.name: M3.4 Shared loading / empty / error / stale states
tasks.details:
OBJ: Dashboards never show a blank white box — every async state has a designed treatment.

STEPS:
1. Loading: skeleton that matches the final chart's footprint (no layout shift), with a delayed spinner to avoid flashing on fast responses.
2. Empty: explains why there's no data (no rows in range vs filters too narrow) and offers a reset action.
3. Error: plain-language message, retry button, and a request id for support.
4. Partial: banner when only some series/panels failed, so the rest still renders.
5. Stale: indicator when data freshness exceeds the expected interval.
6. Implement as a shared wrapper component used by every chart primitive.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Every chart primitive can render all five states via props.
- Layout does not shift between loading and loaded states (measured).
- Empty-state message distinguishes "no data" from "filters exclude everything".

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M3.3's prop contract (can start with it in parallel).

tasks.name: M3.5 Data-fetching, caching & error normalization layer
tasks.details:
OBJ: The data layer between the query APIs and the charts — one place for fetching, caching, and errors.

STEPS:
1. Define typed query functions per metric/endpoint with explicit params (time range, filters, granularity).
2. Implement a query-key scheme so identical requests are deduplicated and cached (e.g. React Query/SWR or equivalent).
3. Set cache/stale policies per metric class: real-time (30s), near-real-time (5m), historical (immutable, long cache).
4. Centralize error normalization: timeouts, 401/403, 5xx map to the M3.4 error states.
5. Add abort-on-unmount and abort-on-filter-change to prevent race conditions and stale renders.
6. Provide a mock adapter so the UI can be developed before the APIs are live.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Rapidly toggling filters issues one request per final state, not one per keystroke.
- Out-of-order responses can never overwrite a newer result (covered by a test).
- Swapping mock ↔ live adapter requires a config change only.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on the API contract from M1.5/M2.6 (mock adapter allows a parallel start).

tasks.name: M3.6 Dashboard layout, filter bar & cross-filtering
tasks.details:
COORDINATION TICKET (not directly executable). Split into:

- M3.6a Responsive grid & three dashboard layouts (10h)
- M3.6b Filter bar, URL state & cross-filtering (12h)

Done when all three boards are responsive, filters round-trip through the URL, and cross-filtering works with correct request de-duplication.

tasks.name: M3.7 Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA) implementation
tasks.details:
OBJ: Charts usable by keyboard and screen-reader users, not just mouse users.

STEPS:
1. Add keyboard focus to every interactive chart element (arrows to move between points/bars, Enter to select).
2. Provide a text alternative per chart: a summary sentence (e.g. "Error rate peaked at 4.2% at 14:00") plus a data-table toggle.
3. Ensure aria roles/labels are correct for chart, series, and legend.
4. Never encode meaning by color alone — pair with shape, pattern, or direct labels.
5. Announce filter/result changes politely via an aria-live region.
6. Run automated axe checks plus one manual screen-reader pass per dashboard.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Zero critical axe violations on all three dashboards.
- A keyboard-only user can filter and read every chart's values.
- Each chart exposes a data-table alternative.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on M3.6.

tasks.name: M3.8 Render performance & component test suite
tasks.details:
OBJ: Charts stay fast with real volumes, and regressions get caught automatically.

STEPS:
1. Set budgets: initial dashboard load < 2.5s on throttled 4G, main-thread long tasks < 200ms, chart re-render < 100ms.
2. Implement large-series handling: downsampling (LTTB) or server-side bucketing above ~2k points.
3. Virtualize or paginate large tables.
4. Add component tests (render + interaction) and visual snapshot tests for each primitive's states.
5. Add a Lighthouse/bundle-size check to CI with a hard fail threshold.
6. Profile all three dashboards and record before/after numbers in the repo.

ACCEPTANCE:
- All budgets met and recorded with the measurement method used.
- Downsampling preserves visible shape (spot-checked against the raw series).
- CI fails on a deliberate ~300KB bundle regression.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on M3.6.

tasks.name: M4.1 Unified query/API gateway + OpenAPI contract
tasks.details:
OBJ: One consistent HTTP surface in front of customer data and log metrics.

STEPS:
1. Specify endpoints: /customers/metrics, /logs/metrics, /logs/timeseries, /health/freshness. For each: params, response shape, error codes.
2. Enforce a shared request contract: ISO-8601 time range, granularity enum, filter object, page/page_size where relevant.
3. Implement server-side timeouts (e.g. 10s), max row caps, and a clear 413/422 when limits are exceeded.
4. Add response caching headers + an ETag for immutable historical ranges.
5. Publish an OpenAPI spec and generate typed clients consumed by M3.5.
6. Add contract tests that fail if a response drifts from the spec.

ACCEPTANCE:
- OpenAPI spec is the single source of truth; generated client compiles.
- A malformed request returns a 4xx with an actionable error body, never a 500.
- Contract tests run in CI.

SIZE: ~2-3 days. Depends on M1.5 and M2.6.

tasks.name: M4.2 Authentication & role-based access control
tasks.details:
COORDINATION TICKET (not directly executable). Split into:

- M4.2a SSO/OIDC integration & role model (10h)
- M4.2b Server-side authorization, row-level scoping & audit (12h)

Done when the role x endpoint test matrix passes and customer-level access is auditable.

tasks.name: M4.3 Environment strategy & seeded sample data
tasks.details:
OBJ: dev/staging/prod behave the same, with reproducible seed data.

STEPS:
1. Define the three environments and their differences (data source, auth, scale) in a short doc.
2. Parameterize all config via env vars/secrets manager; zero hardcoded endpoints or credentials in code.
3. Build a seed-data generator producing realistic-but-synthetic customer + log data (with volume knobs).
4. Make staging a production-like mirror: same schema migrations, same instance class, smaller data.
5. Automate environment provisioning (IaC) so a new environment is one command.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A config audit confirms no secrets or environment-specific URLs in the repo.
- `make seed` populates a fresh environment with enough data to exercise every chart.
- Staging can be rebuilt from scratch in under an hour.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on M4.1 (config surface).

tasks.name: M4.4 Query performance tuning & caching
tasks.details:
COORDINATION TICKET (not directly executable). Split into:

- M4.4a Load-test baseline & query profiling (10h)
- M4.4b Caching, query optimization & graceful degradation (12h)

Done when p95 latency hits the agreed target at 10x data / 50 users and degradation is proven by a forced-slow-query test.

tasks.name: M4.5 CI/CD pipeline with migrations & rollback
tasks.details:
OBJ: Deploys are boring: build, test, migrate, ship, roll back.

STEPS:
1. Pipeline stages on every PR: lint → unit tests → build → contract tests → accessibility checks → preview deploy.
2. Migration step runs before app deploy; migrations must be backward-compatible for one release (expand/contract).
3. Deploy to staging automatically on merge; production on manual approval.
4. Implement a tested rollback: redeploy previous artifact + documented handling of forward-only migrations.
5. Add smoke tests that run post-deploy against the live URL (login, load each dashboard, assert 200 + data present).

ACCEPTANCE:
- A red test blocks merge; a green PR reaches staging without manual steps.
- A release and a rollback are both executed successfully in a rehearsal.
- Post-deploy smoke tests catch a deliberately broken build in under 5 minutes.

SIZE: ~2-3 days. Depends on M4.3.

tasks.name: M4.6 Observability: SLIs, freshness panel & alerting
tasks.details:
OBJ: When the dashboard is wrong or slow, you can tell why in minutes.

STEPS:
1. Instrument the golden signals: request rate, error rate, latency (p50/p95), saturation.
2. Add a data-freshness panel: age of newest customer row and newest log event, per source.
3. Build one dashboard-about-the-dashboard page (or extend the Combined Overview) with these signals.
4. Configure alerts: error rate > 2% for 5m, p95 > 2s for 5m, freshness beyond SLA, ingest job failure.
5. Add structured logs + a request id propagated from UI to query.
6. Run an alert drill for each alert and confirm routing + runbook link.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Each alert fires within one evaluation window in a drill and links to the runbook section.
- A single request id can be traced from browser action to database query in the logs.
- Freshness is visible per data source, not just as a global number.

SIZE: ~2 days. Depends on M4.1 and M4.5.

tasks.name: M4.7 Runbook, user documentation & launch handover
tasks.details:
OBJ: Users can learn the product; on-call can fix it without the original team.

STEPS:
1. Write a runbook: architecture diagram, data flow, top failure modes — ingest stalled, DLQ spike, slow queries, auth errors, stale freshness — each with symptoms → checks → fix → link.
2. Document on-call escalation: primary/secondary, response targets, when to page vs ticket.
3. Write user docs: metric definitions (formula + named owner per KPI), filter behavior, known limitations, expected data freshness.
4. Record a short walkthrough (video or annotated screenshots) covering each dashboard.
5. Run a 30-minute handover session with the receiving on-call owner and capture open questions in the doc.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Every dashboard metric has a definition with a named owner.
- Runbook covers the top 5 failure modes with concrete commands/links.
- Handover completed and acknowledged by the receiving owner.

SIZE: ~1.5-2 days. Final task; depends on M4.6 for alert/runbook links.

tasks.name: M2.3a Parser framework + JSON-lines parser
tasks.details:
OBJ: The parser framework plus the JSON-lines path, working and tested.

STEPS:
1. Define the parser interface: raw line(s) + source metadata in, canonical event or typed parse error out.
2. Implement JSON-lines parser: typed decode, unknown fields preserved into a raw map, missing-field handling.
3. Implement the tolerant-field rule: unparsable field → null + counted warning, never a dropped event.
4. Unit tests: valid line, missing required field, wrong type, nested JSON, unicode, very long line.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Interface is format-agnostic and reused by the sibling ticket.
- All fixture cases produce expected event or expected error code.
- No network/cluster needed to run tests.

SIZE: ~1.5 days.

tasks.name: M2.3b Key=value, regex & multi-line parsers + fixtures
tasks.details:
OBJ: The non-JSON formats plus the fixture corpus that proves all parsers.

STEPS:
1. Implement key=value parser using named-capture patterns configured per source.
2. Implement plain-text/regex parser with per-source patterns.
3. Implement multi-line buffering: attach continuation lines (stack traces) to the parent event, with a max-line guard.
4. Build fixture corpus from M2.1 samples: ≥20 cases per format, including malformed input.
5. Wire fixtures into the test runner with one assertion table per format.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Multi-line stack traces attach to exactly one event.
- ≥20 fixtures per format, each with expected output committed alongside.
- A new source can be added by config alone where the format is regex/kv.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M2.3a for the interface.

tasks.name: M3.3a TimeSeries, Bar & KPI tile primitives
tasks.details:
OBJ: The first three primitives, built on the shared prop contract.

STEPS:
1. Define the common prop contract: data shape, accessors, series config, size, state, aria-label.
2. Build TimeSeriesChart (line + area modes) with shared tooltip and legend.
3. Build BarChart with grouped and stacked modes.
4. Build KpiStatTile: value, delta vs previous period, inline sparkline.
5. Gallery entries per component with realistic mocks and edge cases (1 point, all-null series, 10k points).

ACCEPTANCE:
- All three render from mock data with no dashboard-specific code.
- Props fully typed; no `any` in the public API.
- Edge cases visible in the gallery.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M3.1 and M3.2.

tasks.name: M3.3b DataTable, Sparkline & Heatmap primitives
tasks.details:
OBJ: The drill-down and secondary primitives.

STEPS:
1. Build DataTable: sortable columns, pagination, sticky header, numeric formatting.
2. Build Sparkline for inline trends.
3. Build Heatmap with the sequential palette from M3.2 and a legend.
4. Gallery entries for each, including empty and high-density cases.
5. Document when to use table vs chart for the same metric.

ACCEPTANCE:
- DataTable handles 1k rows without layout breakage (pagination/virtualization hook in place).
- Heatmap legend communicates scale without relying on color alone.
- Each component documented in the gallery.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M3.2 and the M3.3a prop contract.

tasks.name: M2.6a Metric definitions & raw aggregation queries
tasks.details:
OBJ: Agreed metric definitions and the raw aggregation queries behind them.

STEPS:
1. Lock the metric list and write each definition: formula, numerator/denominator, exclusions, owner.
2. Write aggregation queries with consistent bucketing (1m/1h/1d) and a shared filter contract.
3. Implement each metric against the raw event store and validate on a small known fixture.
4. Document the filter contract so the API (M4.1) and UI (M3.5) use identical params.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Every metric has a written definition with a named owner.
- Each query runs correctly against a fixture with hand-computed expected values.
- Filter contract documented in one place, not re-invented per endpoint.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M2.5.

tasks.name: M2.6b Summary tables, percentile correctness & query tests
tasks.details:
OBJ: Make the expensive metrics fast and prove the percentiles are right.

STEPS:
1. Identify which metrics exceed the latency budget when computed on the fly.
2. Materialize those into summary tables refreshed on a schedule (e.g. every 5 min for 1h buckets).
3. State the percentile method (histogram/t-digest), its error bounds, and why it is acceptable.
4. Add query tests asserting p50/p95/p99 match hand-computed values within tolerance.
5. Measure: 30-day range query per metric, record before/after latency.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Every metric returns in under 5s for a 30-day range at realistic volume.
- p95 on the fixture dataset matches the hand-computed value within stated tolerance.
- Refresh schedule and staleness window documented.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M2.6a.

tasks.name: M4.2a SSO/OIDC integration & role model
tasks.details:
OBJ: Users log in with the company identity provider and get a role.

STEPS:
1. Integrate OIDC/SSO with the existing IdP; no custom password storage.
2. Map IdP groups/claims to three roles: viewer, analyst, admin.
3. Implement session/token handling: refresh, expiry, logout.
4. Expose the current user + role to the UI for conditional rendering (cosmetic only).
5. Tests: login succeeds, expired token redirects to login, unknown role falls back to least privilege.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Login works end-to-end in staging with the real IdP.
- Unknown/unmapped users default to no access, not viewer.
- No credentials or client secrets in the repo.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M4.1 for the app shell.

tasks.name: M4.2b Server-side authorization, row-level scoping & audit
tasks.details:
OBJ: Authorization actually enforced where the data is read.

STEPS:
1. Enforce role checks server-side on every endpoint (middleware or guard per route).
2. Implement row-level scoping for customer data at the query layer — inject the scope predicate, never trust a client-supplied filter.
3. Write authorization tests: role × endpoint matrix, plus negative cases with hand-crafted params.
4. Log customer-level data access for audit; expose an audit query.
5. Verify the UI cannot bypass: call each endpoint directly with curl using a low-privilege token.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A viewer calling an admin endpoint gets 403, proven by test.
- A scoped analyst cannot retrieve out-of-scope rows even with crafted parameters.
- Audit records exist for customer-level reads.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M4.2a.

tasks.name: M4.4a Load-test baseline & query profiling
tasks.details:
OBJ: Numbers that tell you where the bottlenecks are, before changing anything.

STEPS:
1. Build a load-test script hitting every endpoint with realistic filter combinations.
2. Seed at 10x current data volume; simulate 50 concurrent users.
3. Record p50/p95/p99 latency per endpoint plus error rate; store the baseline in the repo.
4. Profile the slowest 5 queries and identify the cause (missing index, full scan, bad join, no pruning).
5. Produce a prioritized optimization list with expected gain per item.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Baseline numbers recorded and reproducible with one command.
- Each slow query has a diagnosed cause, not just a number.
- Optimization list ordered by impact vs effort.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M4.1 and M4.3.

tasks.name: M4.4b Caching, query optimization & graceful degradation
tasks.details:
OBJ: Apply the fixes and add the safety net for when queries are still slow.

STEPS:
1. Work the M4.4a optimization list: add/repair indexes, pre-aggregate, enforce partition pruning.
2. Add a server-side cache for expensive aggregates keyed by the full filter set; define TTLs.
3. Define invalidation: TTL plus explicit bust on new data load.
4. Add query timeouts with graceful degradation — serve cached/partial data with a staleness flag instead of failing.
5. Re-run the load test; record improvement and the capacity ceiling.

ACCEPTANCE:
- p95 endpoint latency under target (e.g. 1s) at 10x data and 50 concurrent users.
- Cache hit ratio measured and invalidation documented.
- A forced slow query returns a degraded-but-usable response, not a 500.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M4.4a.

tasks.name: M3.6a Responsive grid & three dashboard layouts
tasks.details:
OBJ: The three board layouts on a responsive grid, with real panels placed.

STEPS:
1. Build the 12-column responsive grid with breakpoints: stack at 375px, 2-col at 768px, 3-col at 1440px.
2. Lay out Customer Analytics, Application Health, and Combined Overview using M3.3 primitives.
3. Place panels with mock data; verify no horizontal scroll at any breakpoint.
4. Decide and document per-panel heights/aspect ratios so charts don't jump between loads.
5. Screenshot each board at the three breakpoints for review.

ACCEPTANCE:
- All three boards render at 375/768/1440 without horizontal scroll.
- Panel placement is data-driven props, not copy-pasted markup.
- Screenshots attached for design review.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M3.3.

tasks.name: M3.6b Filter bar, URL state & cross-filtering
tasks.details:
OBJ: One filter model, shared by every panel and persisted in the URL.

STEPS:
1. Build the filter bar: date range presets + custom, service multi-select, customer segment, environment.
2. Serialize filter state into the URL query string; hydrate from it on load (deep links work).
3. Implement cross-filtering: click a bar or legend entry → narrow sibling panels, show "filtered by" chips, clear-all.
4. Define which panels respond to which filters and document the matrix.
5. Debounce filter changes and cancel in-flight requests on change (uses M3.5).

ACCEPTANCE:
- A deep link reproduces the exact same view for another user.
- Cross-filter updates siblings and chips reflect active filters.
- Rapid filter changes fire one request per settled state, not one per keystroke.

SIZE: ~1.5 days. Depends on M3.6a and M3.5.
